title: Releasing games too fast?
author: Moist_Signal_5080
selftext:
Obviously using ai speeds up the game dev process astronomically. I’m able to go from prototype to fully polished game very fast. My games are play tested and feature complete with tons of iterations. I focus on small experiment games, roughly 2 hours or so to complete. I keep the scope small enough that it doesn’t take months and months to finish. Of course I do have a bigger project in the background that takes much longer. But I’m able to complete these smaller games rather quick.

Obviously there’s a lot of AI backlash, and pushing out games back to back is going to look bad. Reception will immediately be “Slop”, because it was developed with AI and the rate of release will probably make it even worse.

I’m considering just putting them on itch for free with donations, or do a short demo and make the game really cheap. Is anyone else in a similar position?

comments.author: DANGEROUS-jim
comments.body:
"A delayed game is eventually good, but a rushed game is forever bad" - think about this quote in the context of AI. AI speeds up dramatically the process of game development. Why is it getting a bad rap as "slop"? Because a lot of people are still putting their work out too early. Good games takes years to make pre-AI, I don't think that timeframe has yet been cut to a couple of months. We still need hundreds or maybe low thousands of hours of iterations and improvement to polish something that will make people admit it's good at all.

You can put your games out there now for free, or you can keep working on them and revisit that concept next month, or two months from now. Listen to the voice in your head if you are looking at your own game thinking "people are going to call this AI slop" - that might mean you know its not ready to share. IMO we shouldn't share our games until someone would look at them and have to wonder "Is this AI or not?" If you're at that point, publish.

Note: I am largely talking out my ass, just based on the endless posts I've seen where AI game devs are basically asking the same questions. Looking for people to support their ideas, to give them encouragement. What i've seen is that the majority of rhetoric is still toxically anti-AI, but I legitimately feel that will subside as more time goes on. You may not want to be the first to the party then, if your game is your passion project and it would hurt your feelings to see people trashing it, and you, just for having used AI.

replies.author: kesoju83
replies.body:
I couldn't agree more with this comment. The problem with games made with AI right now is that most developers seem focused on finishing and releasing them as quickly as possible, without giving much thought to how much fun players will have or how long they'll stay engaged. As a result, we're seeing a flood of low-quality clones with short playtimes.  
So rather than focusing on how quickly we can make a game and how to sell it, I think we should first ask ourselves how we can give players a truly enjoyable experience. The goal should be to make something so good that people say, “Wait, this game was made with AI?”

replies.author: DANGEROUS-jim
replies.body:
Yep. IMO when you use AI to make a game, you put yourself in the position of Executive Producer / Art Director / Writer of a game studio built on magical elves. If you held and of those titles and had human employees working on your project, you’d have to spend MANY MANY hours in meetings with them, overseeing their work, talking through iterations, etc. Sure, magical elves might slap a bunch of stuff together in their workshop in no time flat, but Santa still needs a whole year before anything ships! lol

But yeah to your point: people are in too much of a hurry to publish their games and get people to compliment them.

“Will people know they are AI?”, that’s hard to say, I’m sure there’s more experienced people than me evaluating that. The voice in my head says, this game is awesome and really to ship! 😂 

I don’t think anyone can call it Slop, as in it’s true definition. Although, just because the AI disclaimer, it will certainly get that anyway. It doesn’t matter if it is objectively a good game, those people just love to hate it.

comments.body: I’m only working on 1 game. It’s a fairly large project for it being my first game. I think depending on the intent of the game, certain games are fine to push out quicker if they’re polished and unique. Others that are more large scale should have a lot more time put into them so they aren’t copy paste of other games. Kind of like scrolling the App Store, I see so many copy paste junk games and it gets tiring. I don’t see a game that’s exactly like mine because I have everything in it made piece by piece. It needs to be a game that I wouldn’t mind playing myself for years and would feel good about inviting others to play as well. I like a sense of community within a game.

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
The free-on-itch-with-donations route makes a lot of sense for small 2-hour experiments. It takes the "is this worth my money" argument off the table, and itch players are used to short, weird games.

One idea if you're worried about release cadence looking like a flood: frame them as a series rather than separate products. Something like "experiment #4" on one itch page or collection, with a short devlog note on what each one was testing. That reads as a deliberate practice project instead of churn, it builds a small following who come back for the next one, and the best-received experiment tells you what to grow into your bigger project.

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body:
My projects I’m referring to aren’t AI assisted, their AI thru and thru. I come up with all the ideas and build a game design doc, then let Claude rip through it on max settings. Having everything pre planned and decided helps with consistency. There’s still always bugs and some awkward things that need adjust afterwards. I do a lot of play testing and walkthroughs, to make sure everything looks and plays good. There’s still small things like maybe layering issues, id I walk in front of something, my character goes behind it, tons of little things like that.

My process usually starts once I have some notes on concept for a game I want to make. Once I have enough detail to put a cohesive though together, I record a voice memo of me rambling every though in my head about it. Just one giant rambling. I copy that transcript and give it to Claude. I tell Claude to help me build a game design doc using my ideas. I always specify to not make any decision without me. I have it give me a list of decisions that need made, either contradictions, oversights or just general holes in my concept. Then I run down them one by one and give concrete answers to them all, never leaving any open ended.

For art direction, I use another game as an example. I never say, “give it a fantasy aesthetic”, that’s sure to give you the most generic and AI looking visuals. I’d instead say “use Hades as reference for visuals”. I never tell it to copy any game 1 for 1, I tell it to use a similar style.

Also my games are all built in a single HTML file, so it can get me a solid prototype in a single 5 hour session. With the full design doc, it’s playable start to finish barring any bugs or mishaps. Then play test and iterating from there over the next 4-6 weeks to refine it.

Quality design and taste is another sub problem but that’s where the human comes in as well as reference material.

I can also make a game a day but spending $100 to put it on Steam. It’s a losing proposition.

What we should do is make an indie AI game company and pool resources. One semi success might finance the entire AI operation.
